title: Baal
description: Semitic title often used in reference to deities
wiki_lead:
Baal (), or Ba'al (), was a title and honorific meaning "owner" or "lord" in the Northwest Semitic languages spoken in the Levant during antiquity. From its use among people, it came to be applied to gods. Scholars previously associated the theonym with solar cults and with a variety of unrelated patron deities, but inscriptions have shown that the name Baal was particularly associated with the storm and fertility god Hadad and his local manifestations. The Ugaritic god Baal (𐎁𐎓𐎍) is the protagonist of one of the lengthiest surviving epics from the ancient Near East, the Baal Cycle.
Known by epithets like "rider of the clouds" and "Victorious Baal", he was associated with rain, lightning, wind, fertility, and kingship, and was often depicted in opposition to sea and death deities like Yammu and Mot. Worship of Baal spread throughout the Levant, Egypt, and the Mediterranean via Phoenician colonization, with regional forms such as Baal Hammon in Carthage. The god was also known as "the mighty one", and "the one without equal" ("there is none above him"). 
The Quran references Ba'al worship, portraying him as a false god opposed by the prophet Elijah (Arabic: Ilyās or Elyas) (Qur’an 37:125). The Quran also mentions Ba'al as a common noun meaning “husband” (Qur’an 2:228, 4:128, 11:72, 24:31). In Levantine Arabic, Arḍ Ba'al (Ba'al land) refers to rain-fed land that relies purely on natural rainfall rather than artificial irrigation.
The Hebrew Bible includes use of the term in reference to various Levantine deities, often with application towards Hadad, who was decried as a false god. In the Hebrew Bible, Baal appears frequently as a foreign or rival deity, with prophets like Elijah opposing his cult, while in early Israelite contexts, the title may have sometimes referred to Yahweh. Depiction as a false god was taken over into Christianity and Islam, sometimes under the form Beelzebub in demonology. Classical sources rendered him as Belus. 
Ba'al (בעל) is the most commonly used Modern Hebrew word for a husband.

Name


Epithets
Baʻal's widely used epithet is "rider (or mounter) of the clouds". (rkb ʿrpt, cf. rkb bʿrbt in Ps. 68:4; Ugaritic rkb ʿrpt.) These are related to Zeus's "gatherer of the clouds" and Yahweh's "rider of the heavens". Like the English word ride, rkb has equine and sexual uses.


Etymology
The spelling of the English term "Baal" derives from the Greek Báal (Βάαλ) which appears in the New Testament and Septuagint, and from its Latinized form Baal, which appears in the Vulgate. These forms in turn derive from the vowel-less Northwest Semitic form bʿl (Phoenician and Punic: 𐤁𐤏𐤋). The word's biblical senses as a Phoenician deity and false gods generally were extended during the Protestant Reformation to denote any idols, icons of the saints, or the Catholic Church generally. In Canaanite mythology, as preserved in Ugaritic texts from the Late Bronze Age city of Ugarit (c. 1450â1180 BCE), Baal served as a warrior deity who controlled rain, thunder, lightning, and agricultural abundance, often depicted as the "Rider of the Clouds " wielding weapons symbolizing natural forces. He was identified as the son of Dagan and operated within a divine council alongside the high god El, ruling as king of the gods after ascending through epic struggles. The primary source for Baal's mythology is the Baal Cycle, a series of six clay tablets unearthed at Ugarit, detailing his battles and seasonal triumphs. In these myths, Baal defeats the chaotic sea god Yamm (using a mace crafted by the artisan god Kothar-wa-Hasis) to establish his palace on Mount Zaphon, symbolizing his dominion over order and fertility. This battle exemplifies the chaoskampf motifâa widespread mythological pattern in which a storm god defeats a sea or chaos monster to establish cosmic orderâseen also in the Vedic Indra's battle with the serpent Vritra. However, these are typological parallels common across ancient mythologies, not evidence of direct borrowing or shared origins; there is no direct historical, etymological, or cultural connection between Baal and Hindu gods or Hinduism, as Baal originates from Northwest Semitic religions in the ancient Near East. Later, he descends to the underworld, where he is slain by the death god Mot, only to be avenged and resurrected by his sister-consort Anat, a fierce warrior goddess; this cycle explains the annual drought and return of rains in the Levant. Baal's attributesâhorned helmet, spear, and thunderboltâappear in iconography, such as a 1.42-meter limestone stele from Ugarit depicting him in dynamic pose, now housed in the Louvre. Baal's worship was widespread in the ancient Levant, from Phoenicia to Syria, influencing local cults and syncretizing with other storm gods like Mesopotamian Adad; temples dedicated to him, such as at Ugarit and Baalbek (ancient Heliopolis), featured high places and altars for offerings tied to agricultural rites. In the Hebrew Bible, Baal appears over 70 times as a rival to Yahweh, with prophetic polemics decrying his cult in Israel and Judah during the Iron Age, reflecting ongoing cultural and religious tensions in the region. His legacy persisted into Hellenistic and Roman periods through assimilated forms, underscoring his enduring role in shaping Near Eastern religious traditions.
